bio_ocra.6.2.summary: These comprehensive revision notes cover the structure and function of the human eye, along with common eye defects and their treatments, tailored specifically for OCR GCSE Biology. You will learn how light enters the eye, how accommodation and pupillary reflexes focus images on the retina, and how corrective lenses or surgery fix myopia and hyperopia. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for mastering coordination and control in biological systems.

core.p: The eye is a highly specialised sense organ containing receptor cells sensitive to light intensity and colour. Each part of the eye has a specific structural adaptation to detect light and transmit impulses to the central nervous system.
bullets: Cornea: Transparent outer layer that refracts (bends) light entering the eye.
Iris: Pigmented muscular ring that controls the size of the pupil and amount of light entering.
Pupil: Hole in the centre of the iris that allows light to pass to the retina.
Lens: Transparent, flexible biconvex structure that fine-tunes the focusing of light onto the retina.
Retina: Inner layer packed with receptor cells (rods and cones) that convert light into electrical impulses.
Optic nerve: Sensory neurone that transmits electrical impulses from the retina to the brain.

callouts.p: The inner layer of the eye containing light receptor cells (rods and cones).
The cornea does most of the initial focusing, while the lens adjusts the fine focus.

core.p: The retina contains two main types of photoreceptor cells that translate light energy into electrical signals, enabling vision in varying light conditions and colour perception.
bullets: Rods: Highly sensitive to light intensity; operate well in dim light but do not distinguish colours; found mostly in the peripheral retina.
Cones: Sensitive to high light intensity and colour; three types responsive to red, green, and blue light; concentrated in the fovea.
Fovea: Central part of the retina with the highest concentration of cone cells for sharp, detailed colour vision.
Photoreceptors synapse with sensory neurones in the optic nerve carrying impulses to the brain.

callouts.p: Cones are concentrated at the fovea; rods are spread across the periphery of the retina.

core.h: Accommodation: Focusing on Near and Distant Objects
core.p: Accommodation is the process by which the eye changes the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects. This involves the coordinated action of the ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments.
bullets: Distant objects: Ciliary muscles **relax**, suspensory ligaments **pull tight (tension increases)**, lens becomes **thin and flat**, light is refracted less.
Near objects: Ciliary muscles **contract**, suspensory ligaments **slack (tension decreases)**, lens becomes **thick and rounded**, light is refracted strongly.

callouts.p: The adjustment of the thickness of the lens to focus on objects at different distances.
Students often mix up ciliary muscle action. Remember: Ciliary muscles contract for near objects (C for C).

core.p: When viewing objects far away, light rays arrive nearly parallel and require less bending to focus precisely on the retina.
bullets: Ciliary muscles relax, increasing the ring diameter.
Suspensory ligaments are pulled taut as tension is applied from the relaxed ciliary muscles.
The elastic lens is pulled into a flatter, thinner profile.
Optical power decreases, allowing parallel rays to converge on the retina.

callouts.p: Always state the state of ciliary muscles first, then suspensory ligaments, then lens shape.

core.p: When viewing close objects, light rays diverge and require significant refraction to converge on the retinal surface.
bullets: Ciliary muscles contract, moving inwards and forwards, releasing tension.
Suspensory ligaments become slack because the ciliary muscles are no longer pulling them taut.
The natural elasticity of the lens causes it to spring into a thicker, more rounded shape.
Optical power increases sharply to bend diverging rays onto the retina.

callouts.p: The lens is elastic, meaning it naturally bulges when tension is removed.

core.p: The iris controls the amount of light entering the eye via an involuntary reflex action mediated by antagonistic circular and radial muscles.
bullets: In bright light: **Circular muscles contract**, **radial muscles relax**, pupil constricts to protect light-sensitive cells from damage.
In dim light: **Circular muscles relax**, **radial muscles contract**, pupil dilates to let as much light in as possible.
Controlled by antagonistic muscle action: when one contracts, the other relaxes.

callouts.p: An automatic reflex protecting the retina from bright light and optimising vision in dim light.

core.p: Myopia is a common vision defect where distant objects appear blurred because images focus in front of the retina rather than directly on it.
bullets: Cause 1: Eyeball is too long.
Cause 2: Cornea or lens is too curved (refracts light too strongly).
Result: Light rays converge before reaching the retina, forming a blurry image.
Correction: Corrected using a **concave (diverging) lens** which spreads out light rays before they enter the eye.

callouts.p: Concave lenses diverge light so it focuses further back, directly onto the retina.

core.p: Hyperopia is a vision defect where near objects appear blurred because images focus behind the retina.
bullets: Cause 1: Eyeball is too short.
Cause 2: Cornea or lens is too flat (does not refract light strongly enough).
Result: Light rays have not converged by the time they hit the retina, causing a blurry image.
Correction: Corrected using a **convex (converging) lens** which pre-focuses light before it enters the eye.

callouts.p: Convex lenses converge light so it focuses further forward, directly onto the retina.

core.p: Beyond traditional spectacles and contact lenses, modern medical technology offers several surgical options to correct refractive errors permanently.
bullets: Spectacles and Contact lenses: Refract light before it enters the eye to compensate for lens or eyeball shape.
Laser eye surgery: Uses lasers to vaporise and reshape the cornea, altering its optical power.
Myopia surgery: Flattens the cornea to reduce refraction.
Hyperopia surgery: Steapens the cornea to increase refraction.
Replacement lens surgery: Replaces the natural lens with a permanent artificial plastic lens (often used for severe hyperopia or cataracts).

callouts.p: Laser surgery and lens replacement carry surgical risks such as infection or permanent damage.

core.p: Examiners frequently test your ability to distinguish between short-sightedness and long-sightedness in terms of causes, focal points, and corrective lenses.
bullets: Myopia = Short-sightedness; image in front of retina; concave lens.
Hyperopia = Long-sightedness; image behind retina; convex lens.
Both are caused by abnormal eyeball length or improper corneal curvature.

callouts.p: Myopia = Many letters = Concave. Hyperopia = Fewer letters = Convex... or My Near City: Myopia Near Concave.

core.h: Required Knowledge Summary for OCR Biology
core.p: Ensure you can recall the exact pathway of light, structural names, accommodation mechanics, and corrective lens types without hesitation.
bullets: Pathway of light: Cornea -> Pupil/Lens -> Retina -> Optic Nerve -> Brain.
Antagonistic muscles: Ciliary & suspensory ligaments (accommodation); circular & radial muscles (pupil reflex).
All key terms defined precisely.

callouts.p: Every bullet point in spec B3.1d-e is covered across these revision notes.

analogy.p:
The eye functions very much like a digital camera. The **cornea and lens** act like the camera's glass lens system to focus incoming light rays. The **iris and pupil** function like the camera's aperture diaphragm, adjusting how much light enters. Finally, the **retina** acts like the digital image sensor or photographic film, capturing the light pattern and converting it into signals. 

Where the analogy breaks down: A camera adjusts focus by physically moving its lens closer to or further from the sensor. The human eye, however, keeps the lens in a fixed position and changes the **shape (thickness)** of the lens via accommodation.

terms.d: The transparent outer layer of the eye that refracts light entering it.
The pigmented muscular ring that regulates pupil size and light entry.
The aperture in the centre of the iris through which light passes.
A transparent, flexible biconvex structure that fine-tunes focusing onto the retina.
The light-sensitive inner layer containing rod and cone receptor cells.
The sensory neurone carrying electrical impulses from the retina to the brain.
The process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects.
Ring of muscle that relaxes or contracts to alter suspensory ligament tension.
Strong fibres connecting ciliary muscles to the lens.
Retinal photoreceptors sensitive to dim light intensity but not colour.
Retinal photoreceptors sensitive to bright light and colour detail.
Short-sightedness where distant objects appear blurry due to light focusing in front of the retina.
Long-sightedness where near objects appear blurry due to light focusing behind the retina.
A diverging lens used to correct myopia.
A converging lens used to correct hyperopia.

mistakes.w: Saying light is focused by the pupil
mistakes.r: The pupil is just a hole; light is focused by the cornea and lens.

mistakes.w: Stating ciliary muscles contract for distant objects
mistakes.r: Ciliary muscles relax for distant objects and contract for near objects.

mistakes.w: Confusing suspensory ligament tension
mistakes.r: Suspensory ligaments are tight when looking at distant objects and slack when looking at near objects.

mistakes.w: Saying rods detect colour
mistakes.r: Rods detect light intensity only; cones detect colour.

mistakes.w: Stating myopia is corrected with a convex lens
mistakes.r: Myopia is corrected with a concave (diverging) lens.

mistakes.w: Confusing where images fall in hyperopia
mistakes.r: In hyperopia, images focus behind the retina.

mistakes.w: Saying the iris is a single muscle
mistakes.r: The iris consists of antagonistic circular and radial muscles.

exam.q: Describe the changes that occur in the eye when a person looks up from reading a book to view a distant bird.
model: Ciliary muscles relax
Suspensory ligaments become taut / tight
Lens becomes thinner / flatter
Light is refracted less
exam.tip: Mention all four structural changes in the correct sequence.

exam.q: Explain why a person with myopia cannot focus clearly on distant objects.
model: Eyeball is too long / cornea is too curved
Light rays are refracted too strongly
Image focuses in front of the retina
exam.tip: State both the cause and where the focal point lands.

exam.q: Name the type of lens used to correct hyperopia and explain how it works.
model: Convex lens / converging lens
Refracts light inwards so it focuses further forward / on the retina
exam.tip: State the lens type and how it alters light path.

exam.q: Explain the role of the iris in bright light.
model: Circular muscles contract
Radial muscles relax
Pupil constricts to reduce light entering
exam.tip: Reference antagonistic circular and radial muscles explicitly.

exam.q: Compare the functions of rod cells and cone cells in the human retina.
model: Rods are sensitive to dim light, cones are sensitive to bright light
Rods do not distinguish colour, cones detect colour
Rods are found across the periphery, cones are concentrated at the fovea
Both convert light energy into electrical impulses
exam.tip: Use comparative language and cover light level, colour, and distribution.

exam.q: State the pathway of light from entering the eye to reaching the brain.
model: Cornea -> pupil/lens -> retina
Retina -> optic nerve -> brain
exam.tip: Keep the steps in chronological order.

exam.q: Describe how laser eye surgery can correct short-sightedness.
model: Uses a laser to vaporise tissue
Flattens the cornea to reduce its focusing power
exam.tip: Mention flattening the cornea.

exam.q: Explain why suspensory ligaments become slack when viewing a near object.
model: Ciliary muscles contract
Moving inwards, reducing the distance to the lens and releasing tension on ligaments
exam.tip: Link ciliary contraction directly to ligament slackness.

exam.q: What type of receptor cells are primarily located in the fovea of the retina?
model: Cone cells
exam.tip: Single mark question requiring precise terminology.

worked.q: A student investigates how pupil diameter changes when moving from a dark room into bright sunlight. Explain the nervous and muscular mechanism causing this change.
steps: Identify the stimulus: increase in light intensity detected by retinal receptors.
State the sensory pathway: impulses sent along sensory neurones to the brain / reflex center.
Identify effector response: antagonistic muscles in the iris act.
Conclude muscle action: circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax, causing the pupil to constrict.
worked.ans: When moving into bright sunlight, light intensity increases on the retina. Impulses travel to the CNS, triggering a reflex where the circular muscles of the iris contract while the radial muscles relax. This causes the pupil to constrict, reducing the amount of light entering the eye to protect light-sensitive cells.

worked.q: A patient is diagnosed with hyperopia. Draw or describe the light ray path before and after correction with a suitable lens.
steps: Identify the defect: hyperopia means light focuses behind the retina.
State the corrective lens: convex (converging) lens.
Describe pre-lens path: diverging near rays focus too late.
Describe post-correction path: convex lens converges light slightly before entry so rays focus directly on the retina.
worked.ans: In hyperopia, light rays entering the eye from a near object converge too late, focusing behind the retina. By placing a convex (converging) lens in front of the eye, the light rays are pre-focused (bent slightly inward), ensuring they converge precisely on the retina.

bio_ocra.6.3.summary: The brain is the central control organ, divided into distinct regions each with specialised functions. Understanding these regions involves investigating brain activity using techniques such as fMRI and EEG, and recognising the limits of medical interventions for brain damage, including the challenges of regeneration and the role of rehabilitation.

core.p: The brain is the main part of the central nervous system (CNS) and coordinates all body activities. It is protected by the skull and three meninges.
bullets: Located in the cranial cavity
Weighs about 1.4 kg in adults
Divided into forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain

callouts.p: The part of the nervous system consisting of the brain and spinal cord.

core.p: Each region contains specialised structures that perform particular tasks.
bullets: **Cerebrum** – largest part; divided into left and right cerebral hemispheres; contains the cerebral cortex (grey matter) for higher functions.
**Cerebellum** – lies under the cerebrum; coordinates voluntary muscle activity and balance.
**Brainstem** – consists of the medulla oblongata, pons and midbrain; controls vital functions such as breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.

callouts.p: The cerebrum contains the **cerebral cortex**, the site of conscious perception.

core.h: 3. Functional areas of the cerebral cortex
core.p: The cortex is divided into lobes, each associated with specific functions.
bullets: **Frontal lobe** – motor control, planning, speech (Broca’s area).
**Parietal lobe** – somatic sensation, spatial awareness.
**Temporal lobe** – hearing, memory (hippocampus), language comprehension (Wernicke’s area).
**Occipital lobe** – visual processing.

callouts.p: Region in the left frontal lobe responsible for speech production.
Region in the left temporal lobe responsible for language comprehension.

core.p: Electroencephalography measures the electrical activity produced by neurones.
bullets: Electrodes placed on the scalp detect voltage changes.
Shows brain wave patterns (α, β, θ, δ).
Useful for diagnosing epilepsy and sleep disorders.

callouts.p: Remember that EEG records **electrical activity**, not blood flow.

core.p: Functional magnetic resonance imaging detects changes in blood oxygenation linked to neural activity.
bullets: Based on the BOLD (Blood Oxygen Level Dependent) effect.
Provides a colour‑coded map of active brain regions.
Non‑invasive, high spatial resolution.

callouts.p: fMRI does **not** measure electrical activity directly; it infers activity from blood flow.

core.h: 6. Limits of treating brain damage – Regeneration
core.p: Neuronal regeneration in the adult brain is very limited.
bullets: Neurons are post‑mitotic; they rarely divide.
Glial scar formation blocks regrowth.
Stem‑cell therapy is experimental and faces ethical issues.

callouts.p: Most brain damage is **permanent**; treatment focuses on rehabilitation.

core.h: 7. Limits of treating brain damage – Surgical options
core.p: Surgery can remove tumours or relieve pressure but cannot replace lost neurones.
bullets: Craniotomy – opening the skull to access brain tissue.
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) – electrodes implanted to modulate activity (e.g., Parkinson’s).
Risks: infection, bleeding, further damage.

callouts.p: DBS treats symptoms, not the underlying disease.

core.p: Therapies aim to maximise remaining function and promote neuro‑plasticity.
bullets: Physiotherapy – improves motor control.
Speech and language therapy – recovers communication.
Cognitive rehabilitation – exercises memory and attention.

callouts.p: The brain’s ability to reorganise synaptic connections in response to learning or injury.

core.h: 9. Practical investigation – Reaction time and brain function
core.p: A simple ruler drop test can infer the speed of neural processing in the brain.
bullets: Measure distance the ruler falls before the subject catches it.
Calculate reaction time using \( t = \sqrt{2d/g} \).
Faster times indicate more efficient neural pathways.

callouts.p: Do not confuse reaction time with movement time; the test measures total time.

core.h: 10. Summary of brain regions and limits of treatment
core.p: The brain’s specialised regions allow complex behaviour, but damage is hard to reverse because neurons rarely regenerate. Investigation techniques (EEG, fMRI) reveal function, while treatment focuses on managing symptoms and rehabilitation.
bullets: Cerebrum – higher functions.
Cerebellum – coordination.
Brainstem – vital functions.
Limited regeneration → emphasis on rehab.

analogy.t: The brain as a corporate headquarters
analogy.p: Think of the brain like a large company headquarters. The cerebrum is the executive suite where decisions are made (planning, language, memory). The cerebellum is the operations department, fine‑tuning the work of the staff (muscle coordination). The brainstem is the facilities team, keeping the lights and heating on (breathing, heart rate). Just as a company cannot instantly replace a senior manager who leaves, the brain cannot quickly replace lost neurons, so the company must reorganise its remaining staff – similar to neuro‑plasticity. The analogy breaks down because a company can hire new staff, whereas the adult brain has very limited ability to generate new neurones.

terms.d: The largest part of the brain, containing the cerebral cortex and responsible for conscious thought, memory and voluntary movement.
A brain region beneath the cerebrum that coordinates voluntary movements, balance and posture.
The posterior part of the brain connecting to the spinal cord; includes medulla, pons and midbrain and controls vital functions.
The outer layer of grey matter of the cerebrum, involved in higher order functions such as perception, thought and language.
Electroencephalography, a technique that records the electrical activity of the brain via scalp electrodes.
Functional magnetic resonance imaging, a scanning method that maps brain activity by detecting changes in blood oxygen levels.
The ability of the brain to reorganise its structure, function and connections in response to learning or injury.
A surgical treatment involving implantation of electrodes to modulate abnormal brain activity.
A barrier of astrocytes that forms after brain injury, inhibiting neuronal regeneration.
Region in the left frontal lobe responsible for speech production.
Region in the left temporal lobe responsible for language comprehension.
Blood‑oxygen‑level‑dependent response used in fMRI to infer neural activity.

mistakes.w: The cerebellum controls conscious thought
mistakes.r: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance; conscious thought is a function of the cerebrum.

mistakes.w: EEG measures blood flow in the brain
mistakes.r: EEG records electrical activity; fMRI measures blood flow.

mistakes.w: Neurons can readily divide to replace damage
mistakes.r: Neurons are post‑mitotic; they rarely divide in the adult brain.

mistakes.w: Deep brain stimulation cures Parkinson’s disease
mistakes.r: DBS alleviates symptoms but does not cure the disease.

mistakes.w: The brainstem includes the cerebellum
mistakes.r: The brainstem consists of medulla, pons and midbrain; the cerebellum is a separate structure.

mistakes.w: Reaction time test measures only nerve speed
mistakes.r: It measures total time (sensory input, processing, motor output).

mistakes.w: fMRI directly records neuron firing
mistakes.r: fMRI infers activity from changes in blood oxygenation, not direct electrical signals.

exam.q: Explain why damage to the brainstem is more likely to be fatal than damage to the cerebrum.
model: Brainstem controls vital functions (breathing, heart rate).
Damage can stop these functions → death.
Cerebrum controls higher functions; damage may cause loss of consciousness but not immediate death.
exam.tip: Mention specific structures (medulla) and the functions they control.

exam.q: Describe two techniques used to investigate brain function and state one limitation of each.
model: EEG – records electrical activity; limitation: low spatial resolution.
fMRI – maps blood flow changes; limitation: indirect measure of activity and expensive.
exam.tip: Use the exact terms ‘EEG’ and ‘fMRI’ and give one clear limitation for each.

exam.q: Outline the main reasons why neurons in the adult brain cannot be replaced after injury.
model: Neurons are post‑mitotic and do not divide.
Glial scar formation blocks regrowth.
Limited stem‑cell niches in the adult brain.
exam.tip: Use the term ‘post‑mitotic’ and mention glial scar.

exam.q: A student carries out a reaction‑time test using a falling ruler. If the ruler falls 0.20 m before being caught, calculate the reaction time. (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
exam.tip: Show the formula and substitute values clearly.

exam.q: State two ways in which rehabilitation can help a person with brain damage.
model: Physiotherapy – improves motor control.
Speech therapy – restores communication.
exam.tip: Use the exact terms ‘physiotherapy’ and ‘speech therapy’.

exam.q: Explain the principle of the BOLD effect used in fMRI.
model: Active neurons increase oxygen consumption.
Local blood flow rises more than oxygen use.
Resulting increase in oxy‑haemoglobin changes magnetic properties.
These changes are detected to produce a colour‑coded activity map.
exam.tip: Mention oxygen consumption, blood flow, and magnetic property change.

exam.q: Compare the functions of the frontal and occipital lobes.
model: Frontal lobe – motor control, planning, speech (Broca’s area).
Occipital lobe – visual processing.
Both are parts of the cerebral cortex but have different specialised roles.
exam.tip: Use the correct lobe names and at least one specific function for each.

exam.q: Why is deep brain stimulation not a cure for Parkinson’s disease?
model: It only modulates abnormal brain activity to relieve symptoms; it does not stop neuronal loss.
exam.tip: Emphasise ‘symptom relief’ vs ‘cure’.

exam.q: List three structures that form the brainstem.
model: Medulla oblongata, pons, midbrain.
exam.tip: Write them in the correct order.

worked.q: Calculate the reaction time for a ruler that falls 0.12 m before being caught.
steps: Use t = √(2d/g).
Substitute d = 0.12 m, g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Round to 0.16 s.

worked.q: A region of the brain shows a 30 % increase in the BOLD signal during a visual task. Explain what this indicates.

bio_ocra.6.1.summary: A reflex action is a rapid, automatic, and involuntary response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought by the brain, serving primarily to protect the body from harm. The pathway taken by electrical impulses during a reflex is known as a reflex arc, comprising a receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone in the spinal cord or CNS, motor neurone, and an effector. Reaction time is the duration taken to respond to a stimulus, which can be investigated experimentally using the required practical PAG B6 ruler drop test or computerised tests.

core.h: Definition and Biological Importance of Reflexes
core.p: Reflex actions are rapid, involuntary, and automatic responses to stimuli that occur without conscious decision-making by the brain. Because electrical impulses travel directly through the spinal cord or brainstem without routing through conscious brain areas, reflex responses happen in milliseconds.
bullets: **Involuntary nature**: Occurs automatically without conscious control or conscious thought from the brain.
**Survival value**: Protects tissues from physical harm or damage (e.g., pulling a hand away from a hot stove or sharp object).
**Rapidity**: Requires very few synapses and short nerve pathways to minimise response time.
**Innate behaviour**: Reflexes are hardwired into the nervous system from birth rather than learned.
**Example reflexes**: Withdrawal reflex (heat/pain), pupil light reflex (protecting retina), knee-jerk reflex (maintaining balance and posture).

callouts.p: A rapid, automatic, and involuntary response to a stimulus that minimises damage to the body without requiring conscious thought.
Reflexes bypass the conscious processing centres of the cerebral cortex, taking the shortest available pathway through the spinal cord or brainstem.

core.h: The Pathway of a Reflex Arc
core.p: The continuous pathway along which electrical impulses travel during a reflex action is called a reflex arc. The sequence is strictly unidirectional and fixed.
bullets: **Stimulus**: A change in the environment (e.g., temperature rise, mechanical pressure, high intensity light).
**Receptor**: Specialised cells that detect the stimulus and convert it into electrical impulses.
**Sensory Neurone**: Transmits electrical impulses from the receptor to the Central Nervous System (CNS).
**Relay Neurone**: Located within the grey matter of the spinal cord or CNS; connects the sensory neurone to the motor neurone.
**Motor Neurone**: Transmits electrical impulses from the CNS to the target effector.
**Effector**: A muscle or gland that carries out the protective response.
**Response**: The action taken (e.g., muscle contraction to move hand, gland secretion of adrenaline).

core.p: Receptors are specialized cells capable of detecting specific energy changes in the surroundings. Effectors are bodily structures that bring about a response when stimulated by motor neurones.
bullets: **Thermoreceptors**: Detect heat or cold (e.g. in skin).
**Photoreceptors**: Detect light intensity and wavelength (e.g. rods and cones in retina).
**Mechanoreceptors**: Detect mechanical pressure, vibration, or stretch (e.g. skin pressure receptors, stretch receptors in tendons).
**Chemoreceptors**: Detect chemical substances (e.g. taste buds, smell receptors, arterial blood pH receptors).
**Muscular effectors**: Muscle tissue contracts in response to motor impulses (e.g. biceps muscle flexing arm away from heat).
**Glandular effectors**: Glandular tissue secretes chemicals or hormones into blood/ducts (e.g. salivary glands, adrenal glands).

callouts.p: Do not confuse receptors with effectors. Receptors detect stimuli and convert them into impulses; effectors receive motor impulses and carry out actions.

core.p: Neurones do not touch one another; they are separated by microscopic junctions called synapses. Impulses cannot jump across synapses electrically; instead, signals cross chemical gaps via neurotransmitter molecules.
bullets: **Electrical impulse reaches axon terminal**: Triggers presynaptic vesicles containing neurotransmitters to move to the cell membrane.
**Exocytosis**: Vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter molecules into the synaptic cleft.
**Diffusion**: Neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the narrow fluid-filled synaptic cleft down a concentration gradient.
**Receptor binding**: Neurotransmitters bind to complementary protein receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
**New impulse generated**: Receptor binding causes sodium ion channels to open, triggering a new electrical impulse in the postsynaptic neurone.

**Unidirectional flow**: Synapses ensure nerve impulses travel in one direction only because neurotransmitters are only stored in presynaptic terminals and receptors are only present on postsynaptic membranes.

callouts.p: A junction between two neurones across which electrical impulses are transmitted by chemical neurotransmitters.
Chemical diffusion across the synaptic cleft is significantly slower than electrical impulse propagation along an axon. Therefore, pathways with fewer synapses produce faster reflexes.

core.h: Reflex Responses vs Conscious Voluntary Responses
core.p: Human actions can be divided into voluntary (conscious) responses and involuntary (reflex) responses. They differ fundamentally in speed, cerebral involvement, and purpose.
bullets: **Voluntary responses**: Involve conscious decision-making in the cerebral cortex of the brain. Signals travel up the spinal cord to the brain, are processed, and motor impulses travel back down.
**Reflex responses**: Bypass conscious cerebral processing. The pathway routes directly through the spinal cord or brainstem.
**Speed difference**: Reflexes are substantially faster because pathways are shorter and contain fewer synapses.
**Awareness timing**: Awareness of a reflex stimulus (e.g. feeling pain) occurs *after* the physical protective response has already taken place.

callouts.p: Always state that the brain *is* informed of a reflex action after it happens (impulses travel up to the cortex via secondary neurones), but the brain does *not* coordinate the initial reflex response.

core.h: PAG B6: Practical Method for Measuring Reaction Time
core.p: Practical Activity Group (PAG) B6 requires students to measure human reaction time using the ruler drop test. This practical assesses visual-motor reaction speeds under controlled conditions.
bullets: **Subject positioning**: The subject sits comfortably with their forearm rested flat on a table top, leaving their dominant hand overhanging the edge.
**Initial setup**: The tester holds a metric ruler (30 cm or 50 cm) vertically above the subject's open hand.
**Zero alignment**: The bottom end (0 cm mark) of the ruler is aligned exactly level with the top of the subject's thumb and index finger.
**Finger positioning**: The subject holds their thumb and index finger a set distance apart (e.g. 2 cm) without touching the ruler.
**Unannounced drop**: Without warning or visual countdown cues, the tester releases the ruler vertically.
**Catching**: The subject catches the ruler between thumb and forefinger as quickly as possible upon visually detecting movement.
**Measurement**: The distance in centimetres on the ruler directly above the top edge of the thumb is recorded.
**Replication**: Repeat the drop 5 to 10 times per test condition to collect reliable data.

callouts.p: The time taken between the presentation of a sensory stimulus and the initiation of a physical response.

core.h: PAG B6: Experimental Variables and Standardisation
core.p: To obtain valid results when investigating a factor affecting reaction time (e.g. caffeine intake, dominant vs non-dominant hand, fatigue), strict control of variables is required.
bullets: **Independent Variable (IV)**: The factor intentionally altered by the experimenter (e.g. intake of caffeine vs water, dominant vs non-dominant hand).
**Dependent Variable (DV)**: The drop distance caught in centimetres, which is converted into reaction time in seconds.
**Control Variable - Starting Position**: Distance zero on ruler must start exactly level with the finger/thumb split every single drop.
**Control Variable - Finger Gap**: Distance between finger and thumb prior to drop must remain constant (e.g. 2 cm).
**Control Variable - Drop Technique**: Same tester must release ruler without giving audio signals or throwing ruler downwards.
**Control Variable - Environment**: Background noise, room lighting, and ambient distractions must be kept uniform across trials.

callouts.p: Practice improves performance over multiple repeats. To prevent practice effects skewing data, subjects should undergo practice trials *before* recording, or counterbalancing should be used.

core.h: Calculating Reaction Time from Catch Distance
core.p: Distance caught on a ruler is an indirect measure of reaction time. Under constant gravitational acceleration ($g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$), distance can be converted directly into time using kinematic physics.
bullets: **Physics Equation**: $d = \frac{1}{2} g t^2$, rearranged to $t = \sqrt{\frac{2d}{g}}$.
**Variable definitions**: $t$ = reaction time in seconds (s), $d$ = distance caught in metres (m), $g$ = acceleration due to gravity ($9.81\text{ m/s}^2$).
**Unit Conversion Step**: Always convert recorded centimetres (cm) into metres (m) by dividing by 100 before applying the formula.
**Non-linear relationship**: Double the catch distance does *not* equal double the reaction time, because distance increases with the *square* of falling time.

callouts.p: GCSE Biology papers will either provide a conversion conversion table or give you the mathematical formula $t = \sqrt{\frac{2d}{g}}$. Remember to convert cm to metres first!

core.h: Sources of Error and Accuracy Improvements in PAG B6
core.p: Practical experiments in human biology inherently carry sources of variability and experimental error. Identifying these enables improvements in precision and accuracy.
bullets: **Anticipation error**: Subject catches ruler prematurely by guessing when it will drop rather than reacting to visual stimulus. *Fix*: Drop ruler at completely random time intervals.
**Measurement error**: Parallax error when reading distance on ruler at thumb height. *Fix*: Ensure eye level is horizontal with ruler at the moment of reading.
**Variability in drop technique**: Tester slightly pushes ruler downwards instead of purely releasing from rest. *Fix*: Use a mechanical clamp and release pin.
**Anomalous results handling**: Identify values far from the mean, exclude them from calculations, and re-calculate mean drop distance.

callouts.p: Always exclude anomalies before calculating mean catch distance. Sum remaining valid drop distances and divide by the number of valid trials.

core.h: Computerised Reaction Time Tests vs Manual Ruler Drop
core.p: While the ruler drop test is accessible, modern experimental biology frequently uses computerised software tests to evaluate reaction times with greater accuracy.
bullets: **Computerised method**: Subject watches a monitor screen and presses a key/mouse button as soon as a colour changes or shape appears.
**Higher resolution**: Computer software measures response times in milliseconds ($1\text{ ms} = 0.001\text{ s}$), whereas rulers are read in millimetres.
**Elimination of human tester error**: Software drops stimulus automatically without physical force or tester bias.
**Randomised intervals**: Prevents subject anticipation by introducing variable delay times prior to visual stimulus.
**Disadvantages**: Requires electrical equipment, software access, and may test finger clicking speed rather than full limb response.

callouts.p: When asked why computerised tests are superior, write: 'Computerised tests have higher precision, eliminate human tester error in dropping, and prevent anticipation by using random stimulus timing.'

core.p: Reaction times vary significantly between individuals and across different physiological states due to changes in chemical signalling speed across central nervous system synapses.
bullets: **Caffeine (Stimulant)**: Increases neurotransmitters in synapses, speeding up nervous transmission and decreasing reaction time.
**Alcohol / Sedatives (Depressants)**: Slows CNS signal processing and delays synaptic diffusion, increasing reaction time.
**Fatigue**: Rested brains transmit signals faster; tiredness slows synaptic transmission and processing, increasing reaction time.
**Age**: Reaction times generally decrease (fastest) in young adulthood and gradually increase with age due to decreased neurone conduction velocity.
**Distraction**: Secondary cognitive loads (e.g. background noise, phone calls) split attention, increasing overall response time.
**Practice**: Repeated trials strengthen specific neural pathways, slightly decreasing reaction time.

callouts.p: Be careful with terminology! 'Decreased reaction time' means you react **faster**. 'Increased reaction time' means you react **slower**.

core.h: Standard Examples of Reflex Arcs in Humans
core.p: Several classic reflex arcs are tested in GCSE Biology questions. Understanding their pathways helps explain how specific receptors and effectors coordinate protection.
bullets: **Withdrawal Reflex**: Pain receptor in skin detects sharp/hot stimulus -> sensory neurone -> relay neurone in spinal cord -> motor neurone -> arm muscle contracts to pull hand away.

**Pupil Light Reflex**: Photoreceptors in retina detect bright light -> sensory neurone in optic nerve -> relay neurone in brainstem -> motor neurone -> circular muscles of iris contract (pupil constricts) to prevent retinal damage.

**Knee-Jerk Reflex**: Stretch receptor in patellar tendon detects stretch from tap -> sensory neurone -> directly to motor neurone in spinal cord (monosynaptic) -> quadriceps muscle contracts to extend leg, maintaining posture.

callouts.p: Spinal reflexes (e.g. withdrawal reflex) route through the spinal cord. Cranial reflexes (e.g. pupil constricting) route through the brainstem, but still bypass conscious cerebral thought.

analogy.p:
A reflex arc is like an automatic fire sprinkler system inside a building. When heat reaches a thermal bulb sensor (receptor), the bulb breaks directly triggering the water valve (effector) without waiting for a human security guard in the control room (the conscious brain) to analyze CCTV footage and press a manual override switch. This automatic local loop saves precious time and prevents building destruction.

Where the analogy breaks down: A fire sprinkler system is purely mechanical, whereas a reflex arc relies on electrical nerve impulses traveling down axons combined with chemical neurotransmitter diffusion across synaptic gaps.

terms.d: A rapid, automatic, involuntary protective response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought by the brain.
The continuous pathway of neurones and synapses along which electrical impulses travel during a reflex action.
A detectable change in the internal or external environment that triggers a nerve response.
A specialized cell or organ that detects a specific stimulus and converts it into electrical nerve impulses.
A neurone that conducts electrical impulses from sensory receptors to the central nervous system.
A neurone located entirely within the CNS that connects sensory neurones to motor neurones.
A neurone that conducts electrical impulses away from the CNS to an effector organ (muscle or gland).
A muscle or gland that executes a physical response when stimulated by motor nerve impulses.
The microscopic functional gap between two neurones where electrical signals are converted into chemical signals.
A chemical messenger stored in vesicles that diffuses across a synaptic cleft to transmit impulses.
The narrow fluid-filled gap separating presynaptic and postsynaptic neurone membranes.
The time interval between the onset of a sensory stimulus and the physical initiation of a response.
The brain and spinal cord, which integrate sensory information and coordinate responses.
A chemical substance (such as alcohol) that slows down central nervous system activity and increases reaction time.
A chemical substance (such as caffeine) that speeds up central nervous system activity and decreases reaction time.

mistakes.w: Students say reflexes do not involve the brain at all.
mistakes.r: Some reflexes (e.g., pupil light reflex or blinking) use the brainstem as their pathway centre, and spinal reflexes send secondary impulses to the brain after the action so you become consciously aware of pain.

mistakes.w: Students confuse 'decreased reaction time' with 'reacting slower'.
mistakes.r: A lower or decreased reaction time means you reacted in fewer seconds, which is FASTER.

mistakes.w: Students state that electrical impulses jump across the gap in a synapse.
mistakes.r: Impulses CANNOT jump across synapses electrically; transmission occurs by chemical neurotransmitter diffusion.

mistakes.w: Students think the ruler drop test measures a reflex action.
mistakes.r: The ruler drop test measures voluntary visual reaction time, NOT an involuntary reflex response.

mistakes.w: Students double catch distance thinking it means double the reaction time.
mistakes.r: Distance increases with the square of time (d = 0.5 * g * t^2), making the relationship non-linear.

mistakes.w: Students include anomalous results when calculating the mean drop distance.
mistakes.r: Anomalous results must be identified, ignored/excluded, and the mean recalculated using only valid repeats.

mistakes.w: Students forget to convert centimetres to metres before applying the formula t = sqrt(2d / g).
mistakes.r: Always divide catch distance in cm by 100 to convert to metres (m) before calculating reaction time.

mistakes.w: Students state that receptors carry out the physical action.
mistakes.r: Receptors detect stimuli; effectors (muscles or glands) carry out the physical response.

exam.q: Define what is meant by a reflex action.
model: A rapid, automatic, and involuntary response to a stimulus without conscious brain control.
exam.tip: Make sure to include both 'automatic/involuntary' and 'without conscious thought'.

exam.q: State two advantages of reflex actions to human survival.
model: Prevents or minimises physical injury/tissue damage.
Occurs extremely rapidly because the conscious brain is bypassed.
exam.tip: Focus on protection and speed.

exam.q: Describe the path taken by an electrical impulse through a reflex arc when a person touches a hot pin.
model: Pain receptors in skin detect heat/pressure and generate an electrical impulse.
Impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord / CNS.
Impulse passes across a synapse via neurotransmitter to a relay neurone, then across another synapse to a motor neurone.
Motor neurone carries impulse to muscle (effector) causing it to contract and pull the arm away.
exam.tip: Name neurones in correct order: Sensory -> Relay -> Motor, and name the effector.

exam.q: Explain how an electrical impulse is transmitted across a synapse.
model: Electrical impulse arrives at the presynaptic membrane/terminal.
Triggers vesicles to release chemical neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft.
Neurotransmitter diffuses across the fluid gap down a concentration gradient.
Neurotransmitter binds to specific receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, triggering a new electrical impulse.
exam.tip: Use the term 'diffuses' and state that neurotransmitters bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

exam.q: Explain why nerve impulses can only travel in one direction across a synapse.
model: Neurotransmitter vesicles are only present in the presynaptic neurone terminal.
Receptor proteins are only present on the postsynaptic neurone membrane.
exam.tip: Address both presynaptic release and postsynaptic receptor location.

exam.q: A student investigates reaction time using the ruler drop test. Describe how the student should carry out the practical to obtain valid results.
model: Subject rests forearm on table edge with open thumb and index finger positioned a fixed distance apart.
Ruler held vertically by tester with 0 cm mark aligned level with top of subject's thumb.
Ruler released without warning; subject catches it between thumb and forefinger as quickly as possible.
Record drop distance on ruler above thumb, repeat multiple times, discard anomalies, and calculate mean distance.
exam.tip: Explicitly mention control variables like fixed finger gap and releasing without audio cues.

exam.q: Explain why computerised reaction time tests produce more reliable and precise data than ruler drop tests.
model: Higher timing resolution measured in milliseconds (0.001 s) rather than centimetres.
Eliminates human error/bias from tester releasing ruler or parallax error in reading.
Random stimulus presentation prevents subject anticipation.
exam.tip: Use precise terms: resolution, human error, and anticipation.

exam.q: Calculate the reaction time of a student who catches a dropped ruler at a distance of 19.6 cm. Acceleration due to gravity g = 9.81 m/s². Use equation t = sqrt(2d / g). Give answer to 2 decimal places.
model: Convert distance from cm to metres: 19.6 cm = 0.196 m
Substitute into equation: t = sqrt( (2 * 0.196) / 9.81 ) = sqrt( 0.392 / 9.81 ) = sqrt( 0.039959 )
t = 0.20 seconds
exam.tip: Remember to convert cm to m first! Showing working gains method marks even if calculation fails.

exam.q: Compare voluntary responses and involuntary reflex responses in humans.
model: Voluntary responses require conscious processing by the cerebral cortex; reflexes bypass conscious thought.
Reflex responses are much faster than voluntary responses.
Reflex pathways pass through spinal cord or brainstem with fewer synapses; voluntary pathways involve complex brain circuits.
Reflex responses are always identical to a given stimulus, whereas voluntary responses can be varied or chosen.
exam.tip: Structure as direct comparisons using comparative words like 'whereas' or 'faster than'.

exam.q: A student investigated the effect of caffeine on human reaction time. Plan an investigation to test if drinking coffee decreases reaction time. Include variables and safety considerations.
model: Select a group of human subjects of similar age/gender and test baseline reaction time using ruler drop or computer test (take 5 repeats per person to calculate mean baseline).
Administer a standard volume of caffeinated coffee to experimental group and equal volume of decaffeinated coffee/water to control group (double-blind design).
Wait a fixed period of time (e.g. 30 minutes) for caffeine absorption into blood.
Repeat reaction time test using identical equipment and setup (same finger gap, starting position, quiet room).
Control variables: room lighting, temperature, noise levels, subject fatigue, and time of day.
Safety/Ethics: Check for caffeine allergies/sensitivities, cardiac conditions, use clean drinking cups, do not serve scalding hot liquids.
exam.tip: A 6-mark practical design must include independent, dependent, controlled variables, step-by-step method, repeats, and safety.

worked.q:
Calculating Reaction Time from Catch Distance
A student catches a ruler at 18.0 cm during a PAG B6 drop test. Calculate the student's reaction time in seconds. Acceleration due to gravity g = 9.81 m/s^2. Use formula t = sqrt(2d / g). Show working.
steps: Step 1: Convert catch distance from centimetres to metres. d = 18.0 cm / 100 = 0.180 m.
Step 2: Multiply distance by 2: 2 * d = 2 * 0.180 = 0.360.
Step 3: Divide by acceleration due to gravity (g): 0.360 / 9.81 = 0.036697.
Step 4: Take square root: sqrt(0.036697) = 0.19156 s.
Step 5: Round appropriately to 3 decimal places: 0.192 s.

worked.q:
Processing PAG B6 Data and Excluding Anomalies
A student records the following catch distances (cm) over 6 trials after drinking an energy drink: 14 cm, 15 cm, 28 cm, 13 cm, 14 cm, 15 cm.
a) Identify the anomalous result.
b) Calculate the true mean catch distance.
steps: Step 1: Inspect data set: 14, 15, 28, 13, 14, 15. The value '28 cm' is significantly higher than all other readings (which range from 13-15 cm).
Step 2: Identify anomaly: 28 cm is an anomaly caused by distraction or poor release.
Step 3: Exclude 28 cm from the mean calculation.
Step 4: Sum valid remaining values: 14 + 15 + 13 + 14 + 15 = 71 cm.
Step 5: Divide by number of valid trials (5): 71 / 5 = 14.2 cm.
worked.ans:
a) Anomaly = 28 cm
b) True mean catch distance = 14.2 cm

worked.q:
Tracing an Applied Reflex Pathway
A person steps barefoot on a sharp drawing pin and instantly lifts their foot. Name each component of the reflex arc and describe its specific role in this scenario.
steps: Step 1 (Stimulus & Receptor): Pain/pressure stimulus detected by pain mechanoreceptors in skin of foot.
Step 2 (Sensory Neurone): Generates electrical impulses and transmits them along leg sensory neurone into spinal cord.
Step 3 (Synapse & Relay Neurone): Impulse crosses synapse via neurotransmitter to relay neurone in spinal cord grey matter.
Step 4 (Motor Neurone): Relay neurone passes signal across second synapse to motor neurone exiting spinal cord.
Step 5 (Effector & Response): Motor neurone carries impulse to leg flexor muscles (effector), causing muscle contraction that lifts foot off pin.
worked.ans: Path: Pain receptor in foot -> Sensory neurone -> Relay neurone in spinal cord -> Motor neurone -> Leg muscle contracts -> Foot lifted.

bio_ocra.6.0.summary: The human nervous system enables rapid communication and coordination between receptors detecting environmental stimuli and effectors carrying out responses. Comprising the Central Nervous System (brain and spinal cord) and Peripheral Nervous System, it processes information via electrical impulses traveling along specialized neurones. Synapses ensure one-way chemical transmission across microscopic gaps between neurones, maintaining control and precision throughout the body.

core.h: Organization of the Human Nervous System
core.p: The human nervous system is a high-speed communication network divided into two main components: the Central Nervous System (CNS) and the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS). Together, they allow the body to detect changes in the environment and respond appropriately.
bullets: **Central Nervous System (CNS)**: Consists of the **brain** and **spinal cord**. It acts as the central integration center, processing incoming information and making decisions.
**Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)**: Consists of all the **nerves** extending from the CNS to the rest of the body.
The PNS continuously carries sensory information into the CNS and transmits motor instructions out to effectors.

head: System Component
Structures Included
Primary Function
rows: Integrates sensory data, makes decisions, coordinates responses
Connects organs, limbs, and receptors to the CNS

callouts.p: The brain and spinal cord, responsible for integrating and processing sensory information and directing responses.

core.p: The nervous system relies on specialized cells to monitor both external surroundings and internal states.
bullets: A **stimulus** (plural: stimuli) is a detectable change in the internal or external environment (e.g., light, sound, temperature, chemical concentrations, pressure).
**Receptors** are specialized groups of cells that detect specific stimuli.
Receptors are often grouped within specialized **sense organs** (e.g., photoreceptors in the eyes detect light; mechanoreceptors in the skin detect touch and pressure).
When a receptor detects a stimulus, it converts the energy into an electrical impulse.

callouts.p: Receptors act as transducers: they convert energy from a stimulus (like light or mechanical pressure) into electrical energy (an electrical impulse).

core.p: Neurones (nerve cells) are highly specialized cells adapted for the rapid transmission of electrical impulses over long distances.
bullets: **Cell Body**: Contains the nucleus, cytoplasm, and cell organelles; controls the metabolic activity of the cell.
**Dendrites / Dendrons**: Branching extensions that receive electrical impulses from other neurones or receptors and conduct them toward the cell body.
**Axon**: A long fiber that conducts electrical impulses away from the cell body toward effectors or other neurones.
**Axon Terminals**: Endings of the axon that release neurotransmitters across synapses.

callouts.p: Remember: **Dendrites/Dendrons** carry impulses **towards** the cell body; **Axons** carry impulses **away** from the cell body.

core.p: There are three primary types of neurones involved in transmitting information within the nervous system: sensory, relay, and motor neurones.
bullets: **Sensory Neurones**: Transmit electrical impulses from **receptors** to the **CNS**. They have a long dendron and a short axon; the cell body is located along the side of the nerve fiber.
**Relay Neurones** (Interneurones): Located entirely within the **CNS** (brain and spinal cord). They connect sensory neurones to motor neurones. They have short dendrites and a short axon.
**Motor Neurones**: Transmit electrical impulses from the **CNS** to **effectors** (muscles or glands). They have long axons and short dendrites attached directly to the cell body.

core.h: The Myelin Sheath and Insulating Function
core.p: Many neurones are covered by a specialized fatty layer that drastically increases the speed of nerve impulse transmission.
bullets: **Myelin Sheath**: A layer of fatty material wrapped around the axon of a neurone.
**Electrical Insulation**: The myelin sheath acts as an electrical insulator, preventing electrical charge from leaking out of the axon.

**Speed of Transmission**: Electrical impulses 'jump' between uninsulated gaps in the myelin sheath (known as nodes of Ranvier). This dramatically speeds up transmission compared to unmyelinated neurones.
Damage to the myelin sheath (such as in Multiple Sclerosis) slows down or disrupts impulse transmission.

callouts.p: Myelin does NOT generate impulses; it **insulates** the axon to make transmission of electrical impulses faster.

core.h: The Pathway of a Coordinated Response
core.p: A coordinated response follows a strict linear pathway through the nervous system from initial stimulus detection to the final physical action.
bullets: **1. Stimulus**: A change in the environment (e.g., bright light).
**2. Receptor**: Specialized cells detect the stimulus (e.g., photoreceptors in retina).
**3. Sensory Neurone**: Transmits electrical impulse from receptor to CNS.
**4. Coordinator (CNS)**: Processing occurs in spinal cord/brain; relay neurones pass impulse to motor neurone.
**5. Motor Neurone**: Transmits electrical impulse from CNS to effector.
**6. Effector**: A muscle or gland carries out the response.
**7. Response**: The resulting action (e.g., pupil constricts or muscle contracts).

callouts.p: Stimulus → Receptor → Sensory Neurone → CNS (Coordinator) → Motor Neurone → Effector → Response

core.p: Neurones do not touch one another directly. They are separated by microscopic junctions called synapses.
bullets: **Synapse**: The physical junction between two neurones, or between a neurone and an effector.
**Synaptic Cleft**: The narrow gap (approx. 20 nanometers) between the presynaptic membrane and the postsynaptic membrane.
**Presynaptic Knob**: The swollen end of the axon of the transmitting neurone, containing mitochondria and **synaptic vesicles** filled with chemicals called **neurotransmitters**.
**Postsynaptic Membrane**: The membrane of the receiving cell, containing complementary **receptor proteins**.

callouts.p: A junction between two neurones across which electrical impulses are transmitted chemically by neurotransmitters.

core.p: Electrical impulses cannot jump across the physical gap of the synaptic cleft. Information must be converted into a chemical signal.
bullets: **1. Arrival**: An electrical impulse reaches the presynaptic terminal/knob.
**2. Release**: The electrical impulse stimulates vesicles containing **neurotransmitter** to fuse with the presynaptic membrane.
**3. Diffusion**: Neurotransmitter molecules are released into the synaptic cleft and **diffuse** across the gap down a concentration gradient.
**4. Binding**: Neurotransmitters bind to complementary **receptor proteins** on the postsynaptic membrane.
**5. New Impulse**: Binding triggers a **new electrical impulse** in the postsynaptic neurone.
**6. Removal**: Neurotransmitters are rapidly broken down by enzymes or reabsorbed back into the presynaptic neurone to reset the receptor.

callouts.p: Diffusion across the synaptic cleft is significantly slower than electrical conduction along the axon. Therefore, pathways with more synapses take slightly longer to transmit signals.

core.p: Synapses ensure that nerve impulses travel in one direction only through the nervous system.
bullets: **Presynaptic Vesicles**: Neurotransmitters are **only stored in vesicles inside the presynaptic neurone**.
**Postsynaptic Receptors**: Specific receptor proteins are **only present on the postsynaptic membrane**.
Because of this structural asymmetry, neurotransmitters can only diffuse from presynaptic to postsynaptic sides, guaranteeing unidirectional transmission.

callouts.p: If asked why signals only travel in one direction: state that neurotransmitter is ONLY released from the presynaptic neurone AND receptors are ONLY on the postsynaptic membrane.

core.p: Effectors are organs that carry out the body's response to a stimulus, restoring optimal conditions or preventing harm.
bullets: **Muscle Effectors**: Respond to nerve impulses by **contracting** (e.g., pulling a hand away from heat, contracting biceps).
**Glandular Effectors**: Respond to nerve impulses by **secreting chemicals/hormones** (e.g., salivary glands releasing saliva, adrenal glands releasing adrenaline).

core.p: The human body uses two major coordination systems: the nervous system and the endocrine (hormonal) system.
bullets: **Signal Nature**: Nervous uses electrical impulses (and chemical neurotransmitters at synapses); endocrine uses chemical hormones carried in blood plasma.
**Speed**: Nervous response is extremely rapid; hormonal response is generally slower.
**Duration**: Nervous responses are short-lived; hormonal responses are usually longer-lasting.
**Targeting**: Nervous impulses travel to highly localized, specific effectors; hormones travel body-wide and affect target organs with complementary receptors.

analogy.t: The Post Office and Email Transmission
analogy.p: Think of electrical impulse transmission along an axon like high-speed broadband internet passing data through a fiber-optic cable. When the data reaches the end of the cable (presynaptic knob), it cannot cross the open air to another house directly. It converts into a physical letter (neurotransmitter), which is dropped across the street (synaptic cleft) to be placed into a specific mailbox (postsynaptic receptor). Once delivered into the mailbox, the house converts the letter back into a high-speed digital cable signal (new electrical impulse). This breakdown occurs because real neurotransmitters undergo active reuptake or enzymatic destruction rather than just sitting in a mailbox.

mistakes.w: Electrical impulses jump across the synapse.
mistakes.r: Electrical impulses cannot cross the synaptic cleft; transmission across a synapse occurs via chemical diffusion of neurotransmitters.

mistakes.w: Brain and spinal cord are part of the peripheral nervous system.
mistakes.r: The brain and spinal cord form the Central Nervous System (CNS).

mistakes.w: Myelin sheath creates electrical impulses.
mistakes.r: The myelin sheath insulates the axon to speed up transmission of impulses; it does not generate them.

mistakes.w: Effectors detect changes in the environment.
mistakes.r: Receptors detect changes; effectors (muscles or glands) carry out the response.

mistakes.w: Sensory neurones carry signals from the CNS to muscles.
mistakes.r: Sensory neurones carry signals from receptors to the CNS. Motor neurones carry signals from the CNS to effectors.

mistakes.w: Neurotransmitters move by osmosis across the synapse.
mistakes.r: Neurotransmitters move across the synaptic cleft by diffusion.

mistakes.w: Impulses can travel in both directions across a synapse.
mistakes.r: Impulses only move in one direction because neurotransmitters are only stored in presynaptic vesicles and receptors are only on postsynaptic membranes.

mistakes.w: Glands contract to produce a response.
mistakes.r: Muscles contract; glands secrete hormones or chemicals.

Spinal cord

exam.q: Name the cell type that detects stimuli in the environment.
model: Receptor (cell)
exam.tip: Make sure to distinguish between receptors (detectors) and effectors (responders).

exam.q: Describe the function of the myelin sheath on a motor neurone.
model: Insulates the axon electrically
Increases the speed of transmission of electrical impulses
exam.tip: Always link insulation explicitly to increasing the speed of the impulse.

exam.q: Explain how an electrical impulse is transmitted across a synapse.
model: Electrical impulse arrives at the presynaptic neurone / presynaptic knob
Causes release of neurotransmitter from vesicles into synaptic cleft
Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic gap / cleft
Neurotransmitter binds to complementary receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
Triggers a new electrical impulse in the postsynaptic neurone
exam.tip: Use key terms: presynaptic knob, vesicle, neurotransmitter, diffusion, receptors, postsynaptic membrane.

exam.q: Explain why nerve impulses can only travel in one direction across a synapse.
model: Neurotransmitters are only present in / released from presynaptic vesicles
Receptors are only present on the postsynaptic membrane
exam.tip: Mention BOTH the presynaptic side (vesicles/neurotransmitters) and postsynaptic side (receptors).

exam.q: Compare the action of muscles and glands as effectors.
model: Muscles respond by contracting
Glands respond by secreting chemicals / hormones
exam.tip: State the specific action verb for each type of effector.

exam.q: Outline the path taken by an electrical impulse from detecting a stimulus to producing a response in a voluntary action.
model: Receptor detects stimulus and generates an electrical impulse
Impulse travels along a sensory neurone to the CNS / brain
Relay neurone passes signal within CNS to a motor neurone
Motor neurone carries impulse to an effector (muscle or gland) to cause a response
exam.tip: List the order strictly: Receptor -> Sensory -> CNS/Relay -> Motor -> Effector.

exam.q: Compare nervous and hormonal communication in the human body.
model: Nervous system uses electrical impulses whereas hormonal system uses chemicals in blood
Nervous transmission is faster than hormonal transmission
Nervous responses are short-lived whereas hormonal responses are longer lasting
Nervous system targets localized specific areas whereas hormonal system targets wider target organs
exam.tip: When asked to compare, provide contrasting statements for both systems across clear categories.

worked.q: A student measures the time taken for a nerve impulse to travel along a 1.2 meter sensory neurone pathway. The impulse takes 0.015 seconds. Calculate the speed of the nerve impulse in meters per second (m/s).
steps: State the equation for speed: Speed = Distance / Time
Substitute the given values into the equation: Speed = 1.2 m / 0.015 s
Calculate the final value: Speed = 80 m/s

worked.q: A neurone pathway consists of two nerve fibers connected by one synapse. Fiber 1 is 0.5 m long (conduction speed = 100 m/s). Fiber 2 is 0.5 m long (conduction speed = 100 m/s). Synaptic delay is 0.002 seconds. Calculate the total time taken for an impulse to traverse the pathway.
steps: Calculate time for Fiber 1: Time = Distance / Speed = 0.5 / 100 = 0.005 s
Calculate time for Fiber 2: Time = Distance / Speed = 0.5 / 100 = 0.005 s
Add time for both fibers and synaptic delay: Total Time = 0.005 + 0.005 + 0.002 = 0.012 s
